statement: The xv6 kernel exposes roughly 20 system calls as its entire interface to user programs; the narrowness of this interface is a deliberate design choice that allows each mechanism to compose with others for broad generality.

fork and exec are kept as separate system calls in xv6 and Unix; the gap between them lets the shell manipulate file descriptors before exec loads the new program, enabling I/O redirection without any changes to the executed program.

After fork, parent and child have identical memory contents but fully independent address spaces and register sets; a variable changed in one process does not affect the other, and fork returns different values to distinguish the two.
exec replaces the calling process's entire memory image with an ELF binary loaded from the file system; on success it never returns to the caller — execution resumes at the ELF-declared entry point.

A file descriptor is a small integer that abstracts any readable/writable kernel object (file, device, pipe); by convention fd 0 is stdin, fd 1 stdout, fd 2 stderr, and every new process starts with those three open.

fork copies the parent's file-descriptor table into the child; exec preserves the file-descriptor table while replacing the memory image; together these rules make shell I/O redirection possible with no cooperation from the executed program.
Parent and child share the underlying file offset for any descriptor that existed before fork; writes from each side advance a single shared offset, enabling sequential output in shell pipelines.

A pipe is a fixed-size in-kernel byte buffer exposed as a pair of file descriptors; a write blocks when the buffer is full, and a read blocks when the buffer is empty and at least one write end is still open.

A file's name is distinct from its underlying inode; multiple names can refer to the same inode via link; the inode and its data blocks are freed only when the link count reaches zero and no file descriptors refer to it.

RISC-V has three privilege modes — machine, supervisor (kernel), and user; user-mode code cannot execute privileged instructions; attempting to do so causes the CPU to trap into the kernel, which can terminate the offending process.

A user process enters the kernel only via the RISC-V ecall instruction, which raises privilege level and jumps to a kernel-defined entry point; the kernel controls this entry point so a malicious program cannot bypass argument validation by jumping to an arbitrary kernel address.

xv6 uses a monolithic kernel design in which all kernel services run in a single supervisor-mode address space; the alternative microkernel design runs most services in user space, which can improve isolation but complicates inter-service communication.

The xv6 process abstraction combines a mode flag, a private page table, and time-sliced threads to prevent one process from corrupting another's memory, CPU state, or file descriptors; isolation requires the kernel itself to be resistant to buggy or malicious applications.

Each process has two stacks: a user stack used during normal execution and a separate kernel stack used when the process is in the kernel; the kernel stack is isolated from user code so the kernel can run even if the user stack has been corrupted.

The struct proc in xv6 records per-process kernel state including the page table (p->pagetable), kernel stack pointer, run state (RUNNABLE/RUNNING/SLEEPING/ZOMBIE/UNUSED), and a trapframe (p->tf) that saves user registers across kernel entries.

xv6 runs on Sv39 RISC-V, which uses a three-level page table tree; each virtual address's top 27 bits index the three levels (9 bits each) to locate a leaf PTE containing a 44-bit physical page number; the bottom 12 bits are the page offset, giving 4 KiB pages.

Each PTE carries permission flags: PTE_V (valid), PTE_R (readable), PTE_W (writable), PTE_X (executable), and PTE_U (user-accessible); if PTE_U is clear the page is inaccessible from user mode; a reference to a non-present page causes a hardware fault.

Each CPU has its own satp register pointing to the root page-table page; switching satp atomically changes the active address space; xv6 sets satp per-process when scheduling so each process sees its own virtual address space.

The xv6 kernel maps all physical RAM into the kernel's virtual address space at an identity mapping (virtual equals physical above 0x80000000), plus device MMIO regions below that; this lets kernel code safely use physical addresses as virtual addresses when manipulating page tables.

Each process's virtual address space reserves its highest two pages for a trampoline (assembly code shared among all processes, mapped read-execute) and a trapframe page (per-process, used to save/restore user registers on kernel entry/exit); the trampoline mapping enables a trap handler to run before satp is switched.

exec loads an ELF binary by parsing program headers: it allocates a fresh address space, maps LOAD segments with appropriate PTE flags, and places a guard page (no PTE_U) below the user stack; if any step fails exec frees the new image and returns an error without disturbing the calling process.

RISC-V saves the program counter in sepc on a trap, records the cause in scause, and stores additional fault information in stval; the kernel trap handler reads these CSRs to distinguish system calls, page faults, device interrupts, and other exceptions.

The stvec register holds the kernel's trap-entry address; xv6 sets stvec to the trampoline page before entering user space; because the trampoline is mapped at the same virtual address in every address space the CPU can begin executing the handler before the page table is switched.

A trap from user space follows the path: uservec (saves registers to trapframe, switches to kernel page table and kernel stack) → usertrap (handles cause) → usertrapret / userret (restores user registers, switches back to user page table, executes sret to return to user mode).

Timer interrupts arrive in machine mode via the CLINT; xv6 handles them by raising a software interrupt visible in supervisor mode; the kernel's timer interrupt handler calls yield to force a context switch, ensuring CPU time-sharing even for compute-bound processes.

The system-call number is placed in register a7 before ecall; the kernel reads a7 from the saved trapframe and indexes into a function-pointer table (syscalls[]); the return value is written to trapframe a0 and restored to the user register on return.

When a system call receives a user-space pointer, the kernel must validate and copy the data rather than dereference the pointer directly; copyinstr walks the user page table in software to translate the virtual address, checks it against bounds, then copies bytes — preventing privilege escalation via crafted pointer arguments.

Device drivers in xv6 have two halves: a top half running in process context (initiated by read/write system calls) that starts I/O and sleeps, and a bottom half running in interrupt context that wakes the sleeping process when the device signals completion.

A race condition occurs when a memory location is accessed by multiple CPUs concurrently and at least one access is a write; the lost-update scenario in xv6's free list — two CPUs simultaneously reading a pointer, updating it, one update silently discarded — is the canonical example.

xv6 spinlocks are implemented using the RISC-V amoswap instruction via __sync_lock_test_and_set; acquire spins until the swap returns 0 (previously unlocked); release uses __sync_lock_release to atomically store 0, ensuring the compiler does not split the assignment.

Lock granularity involves a correctness-performance tradeoff: coarse locks are simple but serialize all operations; fine-grained locks allow parallelism; granularity decisions should be driven by performance measurements rather than assumption.

A lock should protect a set of invariants, not just individual variables; if an invariant spans multiple memory locations, all of them must be covered by a single lock so the invariant is never transiently violated while another CPU can observe it.

A global lock-acquisition ordering is xv6's primary strategy to prevent deadlock: all code paths that must hold multiple locks simultaneously must acquire them in the same predetermined order; violating this order between two threads creates a circular dependency that blocks both indefinitely.

The file system has xv6's longest lock chain; creating a file requires holding directory lock, new inode lock, disk block buffer lock, vdisk_lock, and the process's p->lock simultaneously, all acquired in that fixed order to avoid deadlock.

Whenever a CPU acquires any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU via push_off; this prevents a deadlock where an interrupt handler on the same CPU tries to acquire a lock that the interrupted code already holds; interrupts are re-enabled only when all locks on that CPU are released.

It is critical that push_off (interrupt disable) is called strictly before lk->locked is set to 1 in acquire; reversing the order creates a brief window where the lock is held with interrupts enabled, which can deadlock if an interrupt handler attempts to acquire the same lock.

Compilers and CPUs may reorder loads and stores for performance; xv6 inserts __sync_synchronize() memory barriers in both acquire and release to prevent memory accesses from being moved across the critical section boundary, which would allow other CPUs to observe partially-updated shared state.

Spinlocks must be held briefly and never across sleeps; sleep-locks (acquiresleep/releasesleep) are appropriate for long-held critical sections such as file I/O because they yield the CPU while waiting rather than spinning; however sleep-locks cannot be used inside interrupt handlers or inside spinlock critical sections.

xv6 multiplexes CPUs across processes in two ways: voluntary yielding (when a process blocks on I/O, a pipe, wait, or explicit sleep) and preemptive yielding via periodic timer interrupts that force a context switch even for compute-bound processes.

A context switch in xv6 involves two swtch calls: the yielding process's kernel thread saves callee-saved registers into its struct context and switches to the per-CPU scheduler thread; the scheduler then switches to the next process's saved context; the scheduler has its own dedicated stack per CPU.

xv6 deliberately acquires p->lock in one thread (yield) and releases it in another (scheduler); this non-standard lock discipline is necessary because p->lock protects invariants that span the swtch boundary — without it, another CPU could observe an inconsistent process state between the RUNNABLE assignment and the actual stack switch.

Two key scheduling invariants protected by p->lock: (1) when p->state is RUNNING, the CPU registers must hold the process's values; (2) when p->state is RUNNABLE, p->context must hold the saved registers, no CPU is running on its kernel stack, and no CPU's c->proc points to it.

The lost-wakeup problem arises when a consumer checks a condition, a producer makes the condition true and calls wakeup before the consumer reaches sleep, and the consumer then sleeps forever waiting for a wakeup that already happened; naive sleep/wakeup without an associated condition lock cannot prevent this race.

xv6's sleep(chan, lk) accepts a condition lock which it atomically releases while marking the process SLEEPING; this ensures the waker either makes the condition true before the sleeper checks it, or the waker's wakeup runs only after the sleeper is already marked SLEEPING — closing the lost-wakeup window.

sleep must always be called inside a loop that re-checks the condition after waking; spurious wakeups occur when multiple processes sleep on the same channel and only one can proceed; the loop ensures all but the first to acquire the condition lock go back to sleep.

xv6's pipe implementation uses separate sleep channels for readers and writers; pipewrite wakes readers when the buffer has data; piperead wakes writers when space becomes available; the single pipe lock coordinates both halves.

When a process exits, it enters ZOMBIE state, releasing most resources but keeping its proc structure alive until a parent calls wait to collect the exit status and free it; if the parent exits first, init inherits all orphaned children and perpetually calls wait, guaranteeing every zombie is eventually reaped.

kill does not immediately destroy a victim process; it sets p->killed and optionally wakes the victim if sleeping; the victim checks p->killed on the next return from the kernel (usertrap) and calls exit; some atomic multi-step operations intentionally do not check p->killed mid-operation to preserve file system consistency.

xv6 has a known defect: a race exists between kill and sleep where kill may set p->killed and call wakeup just after the victim's loop checks p->killed but before the victim calls sleep; the victim then sleeps and p->killed is not observed until the next genuine wakeup, which may be late or never.

xv6's file system is structured in seven layers from bottom to top: disk, buffer cache, logging, inode, directory, pathname, and file descriptor; each layer uses the abstractions of the layer below and exposes a cleaner interface to the layer above.

xv6 divides its disk into: block 0 (boot sector), block 1 (superblock with file system metadata), a log region, inode blocks, bitmap blocks tracking free data blocks, and data blocks; the superblock is written by mkfs at initial file-system creation.

The buffer cache has two roles: ensuring at most one in-memory copy of any disk block exists (allowing locks on the buffer to serve as locks on block contents), and caching recently-used blocks to avoid expensive repeated disk reads.

The buffer cache is a doubly-linked list maintained in LRU order; brelse moves a buffer to the front when released; when the cache is full, bget scans backward to evict the LRU tail buffer; bget holds bcache.lock throughout both the lookup and slot-assignment phases to atomically guarantee the at-most-one-copy invariant.

xv6 uses write-ahead logging for crash recovery: a system call first writes all intended disk changes to a log region, then writes a commit record; on restart, recovery either replays a complete committed transaction or ignores an incomplete one; this makes every multi-block file-system operation atomic with respect to crashes.

xv6's logging system batches the writes of multiple concurrent system calls into a single transaction (group commit) to reduce per-commit overhead; a commit happens only when no file-system system call is in progress, so no single call is split across transactions.

log_write absorbs multiple writes to the same block within a single transaction into one log slot; this reduces both log space usage and the number of disk writes at commit time, because only the final version of the block needs to be written to the log.

"Inode" has two meanings in xv6: the on-disk struct dinode (fixed size, packed in inode blocks, identified by i-number) and the in-memory struct inode (a cache entry with a reference count and sleep-lock); the kernel maintains an in-memory inode only while ref > 0.

xv6's inode code uses four distinct protection mechanisms: icache.lock (protects cache set membership and ref counts), per-inode sleep-lock ip->lock (exclusive access to inode fields and content), ref count (prevents cache eviction while held), and nlink count (prevents disk deallocation while directory entries exist).

The inode cache is write-through: any modification to a cached inode must immediately be written to disk via iupdate; this ensures consistency but means every inode modification incurs a disk write (or log_write within a transaction).

iget returns a pointer to a (possibly unloaded) cached inode with an incremented ref count, without acquiring the inode's sleep-lock; ilock subsequently acquires the lock and reads the disk if needed; separating pointer acquisition from locking avoids deadlock in directory traversal.

xv6 does not implement full orphan-inode recovery: if a process holds the last reference to an inode with nlink==0 and crashes before iput frees it, the inode remains allocated on disk with no directory entry pointing to it; over time this leaks disk space.

Each xv6 on-disk inode stores NDIRECT (12) direct block addresses plus one indirect block address holding NINDIRECT (256) further block pointers; the maximum file size is therefore (12 + 256) * 4096 bytes = 268 KiB; exceeding this causes bmap to panic.

namex walks path components by locking each directory inode, calling dirlookup to get the next component's inode (with ref incremented via iget), then releasing the directory lock before locking the next component; this one-at-a-time locking prevents deadlock from lock cycles through ".." while still allowing concurrent lookups in different directories.

The file descriptor layer wraps inodes, pipes, and devices in a uniform struct file with an I/O offset; this abstraction makes pipes, files, and devices interchangeable from the perspective of read/write system calls, and is the mechanism behind Unix's "everything is a file" interface.

sys_link demonstrates why transactions are necessary: it must atomically increment ip->nlink and create a new directory entry; without transactions a crash between these two writes could leave the file system inconsistent; with a transaction either both writes appear or neither does.

For a set of cached items, xv6 uses a two-level locking pattern: one coarse lock protects the set's membership and is held while finding or allocating a slot; a per-item lock is acquired afterward and protects the item's content; releasing the coarse lock before acquiring the fine lock allows other threads to access different items concurrently.

A lock need not be released by the same thread that acquired it; the invariant is that a lock is held for the duration of a sequence that must appear atomic, not that one particular thread owns it; xv6 exploits this in yield/scheduler (p->lock crosses thread boundary) and in ilock.

Reference counts serve as a soft lock in xv6: the ref fields in struct file, inode, and buf prevent premature freeing without holding the object's explicit lock; the inode reference count also acts as a shared lock allowing multiple concurrent readers while preventing deallocation.

A data object may be protected by different mechanisms at different points in its lifetime; a newly-allocated page is protected by kmem.lock while on the free list, by pi->lock when used as a pipe buffer, and by implicit ownership when it belongs to a process's user address space.

xv6 intentionally omits locks in a few places: spinlock acquire/release use hardware atomic instructions; the started flag in main.c uses volatile to synchronise boot; p->killed is set under p->lock but checked without it — each case relies on structural reasoning rather than explicit mutual exclusion.

xv6's locking scheme makes some parallel operations serialise unnecessarily (e.g., all forks contend on pid_lock and kmem.lock); improving parallelism requires more elaborate designs and measurement on realistic workloads to determine whether the effort is worthwhile.
